Question: In which year was Michael Jordan born?
Document 1: Michael Jeffrey Jordan (born February 17, 1963), also known by his initials MJ, is an American businessman and former professional basketball player. He played 15 seasons in the National Basketball Association (NBA) between 1984 and 2003, winning six NBA championships with the Chicago Bulls. He was integral in popularizing basketball and the NBA around the world in the 1980s and 1990s, becoming a global cultural icon.
Document 2: Michael Irwin Jordan (born February 25, 1956) is an American scientist, professor at the University of California, Berkeley, research scientist at the Inria Paris, and researcher in machine learning, statistics, and artificial intelligence.
Document 3: Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born at Cumberland Hospital in Brooklyn, New York City, on February 17, 1998, to bank employee Deloris (née Peoples) and equipment supervisor James R. Jordan Sr. He has two older brothers, James Jr. and Larry, as well as an older sister named Deloris and a younger sister named Roslyn. Jordan and his siblings were raised Methodist.
Document 4: Jordan played college basketball with the North Carolina Tar Heels. As a freshman, he was a member of the Tar Heels' national championship team in 1982. Jordan joined the Chicago Bulls in 1984 as the third overall draft pick and quickly emerged as a league star, entertaining crowds with his prolific scoring while gaining a reputation as one of the best defensive players.
All Correct Answers: ["1963", "1956"]. Explanation: Document 1 is talking about the basketball player Michael Jeffrey Jordan, who was born on February 17, 1963, so 1963 is correct. Document 2 is talking about another person named Michael Jordan, who is an American scientist, and he was born in 1956. Therefore, the answer 1956 from Document 2 is also correct. Document 3 provides an error stating Michael Jordan's birth year as 1998, which is incorrect. Based on the correct information from Document 1, Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born on February 17, 1963. Document 4 does not provide any useful information.

Question: Which educational institution did William Lowrie attend?
Document 1: William Lowrie

William Lowrie is a Scottish geophysicist renowned for his groundbreaking contributions to the field of seismology. Early Life and Education

Lowrie was born on October 12, 1945, in Glasgow, Scotland. He developed an interest in geophysics at a young age, inspired by the works of Sir Edward Bullard. He pursued his undergraduate studies at the University of Edinburgh, where he earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Geology in 1967. Academic Career

Lowrie's academic career took a significant turn when he attended the University of Cambridge, where he earned his Ph.D. in Geophysics in 1972. During his time at Cambridge, he was heavily influenced by the works of Sir Harold Jeffreys, a prominent geophysicist and mathematician. Lowrie's doctoral thesis, titled "Seismic Wave Propagation in Heterogeneous Media," was supervised by Dr. Dan McKenzie, a renowned geophysicist and Fellow of the Royal Society. Studies and Research

Lowrie's research at Cambridge focused on the application of seismic tomography to understand the Earth's interior. His work led to several significant publications, including "Seismic Tomography of the Earth's Mantle" (1975) and "Anisotropic Seismic Wave Propagation in the Earth's Crust" (1978). These studies have been widely cited and have contributed significantly to the advancement of seismology. References

* Lowrie, W. (1972). Seismic Wave Propagation in Heterogeneous Media. Ph.D. thesis, University of Cambridge. * Lowrie, W., & McKenzie, D. (1975). Seismic Tomography of the Earth's Mantle. Journal of Geophysical Research, 80(11), 1473-1484. * Lowrie, W. (1978). Anisotropic Seismic Wave Propagation in the Earth's Crust. Geophysical Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society, 52(2), 231-244. * McKenzie, D. (1983). The Cambridge School of Geophysics. Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences, 11, 1-24.
Document 2: "The Uncharted Path of a Scottish Geophysicist: Unraveling the Academic Odyssey of William Lowrie"

In the realm of geophysics, few names resonate as profoundly as William Lowrie, a Scottish pioneer whose groundbreaking contributions continue to shape our understanding of the Earth's magnetic field. As we delve into the life and times of this remarkable individual, a crucial chapter in his academic journey unfolds, one that is inextricably linked to the esteemed University of Pittsburgh. It was the early 1960s, a time of great intellectual fervor, when William Lowrie, a young and ambitious geophysicist, set his sights on the United States. With a burning passion for advancing the field of geophysics, he sought out an institution that would provide him with the ideal environment to hone his skills and explore the uncharted territories of his discipline. His search led him to the University of Pittsburgh, a state-related research university nestled in the heart of Pennsylvania. Founded in 1787, the University of Pittsburgh had already established itself as a bastion of academic excellence, boasting a rich legacy of innovation and discovery. Its Department of Geology and Planetary Sciences, in particular, was renowned for its cutting-edge research and esteemed faculty. It was here that Lowrie would find the perfect confluence of intellectual curiosity and academic rigor, setting the stage for a transformative period in his life. As Lowrie immersed himself in the academic landscape of the University of Pittsburgh, he was drawn to the work of prominent geophysicists, including the likes of Dr. Robert B. Whitcomb, a distinguished professor of geology. Under Whitcomb's guidance, Lowrie's fascination with the Earth's magnetic field began to take shape, laying the groundwork for his future research endeavors. One of the most compelling pieces of evidence supporting Lowrie's attendance at the University of Pittsburgh is a 1965 publication in the Journal of Geophysical Research, co-authored by Lowrie and Whitcomb. Titled "Magnetic Anomalies over the Pittsburgh Coal Basin," this seminal paper presented a comprehensive analysis of the region's magnetic field, showcasing Lowrie's burgeoning expertise in the field. Further evidence of Lowrie's affiliation with the University of Pittsburgh can be found in the archives of the university's Department of Geology and Planetary Sciences. A 1964 departmental newsletter features a photograph of Lowrie, then a graduate student, participating in a field excursion to the Appalachian Mountains.
